schools.summary: Gregory the Great: reproaches are sorer than scourges; that no temptation be lacking, the friends' words gall Job worse than his pains, yet he answered aright, and his few excessive words must be weighed by the Most High Judge who called him perfect.
Gill: Job heard Eliphaz out patiently despite much that was provoking, and now claims only every man's right to answer for himself when his good name is attacked.
Henry: those who would judge a discourse must hear it entire; Job heard Eliphaz to the end and only then replies, speaking very feelingly.
Clarke frames the whole reply: Job vindicates himself, his great affliction being the true cause of his complaining.
Ellicott: Job replies with the despair of a man baulked of sympathy; no formal logical answer, only a reiterated complaint and a longing for one who can enter into it.

Keil and Delitzsch: 'vexation' (kaas) is Eliphaz's own reproach (Job 5:2), to be weighed against Job's 'calamity,' a word from a root meaning to yawn — a gulf, a chasm; the verb pictures the balance-beam sinking.
Clarke: Job asks to be dealt with by strict justice — sins weighed against sufferings, or sufferings against complaints; Wesley hears a longing for an equal judge who would understand his case.
Gill notes the intensive 'in weighing weighed' and the range of the word — grief, wrath, complaint, impatience — wishing it weighed by moderate men who would make allowance.
Henry: unable to describe his calamity, Job would appeal to a third person with just weights and balances to weigh it impartially.

themes: a plea to be measured before condemned

schools.summary: Gill presses the hyperbole — heavier than all the sand of all the seas — yet qualifies that God's people's afflictions are light beside sin's desert, hell, Christ's sufferings, and the weight of glory.

Clarke: the sand is beyond counting for number and estimating for weight, and Job's calamity is both; Wesley reads 'swallowed up' as voice and spirit failing, words insufficient to express the sorrow.
Ellicott: 'swallowed up' means words are useless and powerless to express it; Keil and Delitzsch render instead 'therefore my words are rash,' the burden making his speech unmeasured.

debates.question: What does the closing clause mean — 'my words are swallowed up'?

sides.position: words fail — language is powerless to express so great a grief
'my words are rash' — the hugeness of the burden makes his speech unmeasured

themes: heavier than the sand of the sea

schools.summary: Gill allows the arrows may be outward calamities but presses the inward anguish and sense of divine displeasure — swift, secret, sharp shafts from the bow of God, not dealing with him as a father.

Clarke reads poisoned arrows, burning fever, and parching thirst, citing Aaly's saying that from God the Archer men can flee only to God; Wesley: arrows dipped in God's wrath, the poison drinking up the soul, the terrors an army — Job a type of Christ (John 12:27; Matt. 27:46).

Ellicott corrects the ambiguous AV: rather 'the poison whereof my spirit imbibeth,' the terrors setting themselves 'in array' like marshalled hosts; Keil and Delitzsch render likewise, 'the terrors of Eloah set themselves in array against me.'
Henry: it is God's power above man's that his arrows reach the very soul; trouble of mind is the sorest trouble, a wounded spirit none can bear.

debates.question: How should 'the poison whereof drinketh up my spirit' be rendered?

sides.position: the poison drinks up / consumes his spirit (the received sense)
'the poison whereof my spirit imbibeth' — his own soul drinks in the venom (AV ambiguous)

schools.summary: Gill: the ass and ox complain only in want; were Job silent under real want he would be more senseless than the brutes — an answer to the charge that he complains now though silent in prosperity.

Clarke fixes 'pere,' the wild ass or onager, and presses the challenge — do I complain without cause? the beasts are quiet when fed; Wesley: no wonder the friends, living in ease, complain not, any more than Job did while he wanted nothing.
Henry: in prosperity Job did not bray over his grass, but stripped of all comforts he must be a stock or stone to feel no grief.

themes: the wild ass and the ox
complaint wrung out by real want

schools.summary: Gill gives both readings — the unsavoury food figures the wormwood and gall Job is now fed, or the insipid unsalted talk of Eliphaz.

Clarke reports many construals, settling on Mr. Good's — insipid food yields no pungency, as Job's loathed portion is his very calamity — and notes the rival 'juice of purslain' and 'drivel of dreams'; Wesley keeps the simplest sense of bitter meat.
Ellicott notes the same lexical doubt — 'the white of an egg' taken by some as 'the juice of purslain' — while agreeing Job's soul refuses the tasteless remedies as loathsome meat.
Henry blends the two: the egg-white is at once Job's poorest dish and the friends' sapless, insipid comfort, loathsome when applied to his wounds.

debates.question: Do the tasteless food-images describe Job's bitter affliction or the friends' insipid comfort?

sides.position: his own loathsome portion under God's hand
the friends' sapless words and comfort

debates.question: What is 'the white of an egg'?

sides.position: the white of an egg
the juice of purslain (a lexical alternative)

schools.summary: Gill again gives two readings, preferring the second: the loathsome food now his only fare, or (rather) the friends' insipid words, refused and nauseated like tainted meat.
Wesley reads a third sense: the dreaded afflictions Job once could not bear to think of are now his daily, sorrowful bread.
Henry keeps to the food and draws the lesson not to be nice and dainty, since necessity may make the once-scorned dish acceptable.

debates.question: What are 'the things my soul refused to touch'?

sides.position: the loathsome food or comfort he must now swallow
the dreaded afflictions become his daily bread

schools.summary: Gill: the one thing uppermost in Job's mind is death, imagined as a person who looks in at the windows and enters the houses of men.
Henry: passion grows violent when checked; Job repeats the death-wish more vehemently, yet never offers to destroy himself — the soul must not break prison but wait for a fair discharge.
Clarke: having no hope of redemption from his helpless state, Job asks God to shorten it by taking his life.

Ellicott: baffled among men, Job turns to God as his only hope — rather from God than in God — looking to death when years of life were yet in store (cf. Job 17); Keil and Delitzsch fix the paradox that not life but death is his expectation.

themes: oh that I might have my request
the paradox of death as hope

schools.summary: Gill guards the word: not everlasting destruction of soul and body, but the dissolution of the body — his house of clay crushed to powder and returned to dust (Broughton: 'to the dust of death').

Keil and Delitzsch take 'cut me off' of the thread of life (cf. Isa. 38:12) and note the piled optatives; Ellicott owns the sequence obscure and the clause 'harden myself in sorrow' the most doubtful in the passage, occurring nowhere else.
Clarke reads 'let loose his hand' as the archer loosing his hold that the arrow may fly (cf. v.4); Wesley: to destroy is to end his days and calamities together.
Henry hears the mercy-stroke — God who made him poor and sick asked to strike once more — the destruction once a terror (Job 31:23) now courted, in hope the spirit be saved.
Gill weighs comfort before death (exulting on the brink, 'O death, where is thy sting?') or after it (no temporal comfort left, but God's presence beyond the grave).

Clarke opens the variant 'This' for 'yet' (Vulgate, Chaldee, MSS), reads 'harden myself' as determinate resolution and 'let him not spare' as non-resistance; Wesley: courage borrowed from hope of blessedness after death, 'not concealed' meaning he boldly professed true religion among the heathen.
Henry makes the clear conscience the whole ground of comfort: Job neither kept God's words from himself nor to himself; only those good and doing good may promise comfort in death.
Ellicott: to 'conceal' is to deny, Job's confidence the Psalmist's (Ps. 40:9-10); Keil and Delitzsch render the trembling line 'I would exult in unsparing pain,' the confession standing unbroken.

sides.position: 'Then should I YET have comfort' (received text)
'THIS should be my comfort' (variant, with Vulgate and Chaldee)

themes: then should I yet have comfort
the words of the Holy One
comfort grounded in fidelity, not innocence

schools.summary: Gill reads the first question against Eliphaz's promised recovery of health, the word bearing also 'that I should bear' the load or endure.

Keil and Delitzsch: is not Job's strength so wasted and his end so certain that long waiting is both impossible and useless? — 'prolong my life' literally to draw out the soul, i.e. be patient; Ellicott notes the same alternative of 'be patient.'

Clarke: Job can never suppose his strength restored, and no happy end is in prospect; Wesley turns the second question — what is death to me? not terrible but comfortable — while noting Job never offered to end his own life.
Henry meditates on frail strength — depending, decaying, disproportionate — so that we should wonder we have lived till now, and the ready soul sees little to invite its stay.

themes: what is my strength that I should hope
prolong my life or be patient

schools.summary: Gill: is Job's strength like foundation-stones or a load-bearing pillar? It is not, and he cannot sustain the burden.

Clarke calls it a proverb found in all countries, citing Cicero (man not chiselled from rock nor hewn from oak) and Homer's Iliad (bodies not rock nor ribbed with steel); Wesley: Job is flesh and blood, unable to endure longer.
Keil and Delitzsch let the couplet stand in the run of questions by which Job proves his helplessness.
Henry: are his muscles brass and sinews steel? No; he cannot hold out but must sink under the load.

themes: strength of stones, flesh of brass
the cruelty of demanding granite patience

schools.summary: Gill affirms resource still remaining: his help and defence are in his own power — a good conscience and the force of argument to answer the calumnies.
Henry: Job guards against the charge of raving — he has the use of his reason, is 'not mad, most noble Eliphaz,' and has a light within that helps in the worst of times.

Wesley gives the affirmation its sharpest form — granting his outward state hopeless, has he lost his understanding? Clarke leans the other way: his help is all in himself and perfect weakness, his 'subsistence' driven from him, though (he insists) his reason is not.

Keil and Delitzsch turn the question to a confession of collapse — 'am I not utterly helpless, and continuance driven from me?'; Ellicott owns the obscurity and offers both an affirming and a despairing sense.

debates.question: Does the verse affirm Job's remaining resource or confess his utter helplessness?

sides.position: help and wisdom still within — reason and conscience to plead his cause
a confession of total helplessness, his last stay driven from him

themes: is not my help in me

schools.summary: Gill: the afflicted man is the natural object of pity — sympathy expressed in visiting, comforting, and relieving, as the law of friendship requires.
Henry: compassion is a debt owed the afflicted, and inhumanity is impiety — he that withholds pity 'forsakes the fear of the Almighty' (so the Chaldee), echoing 1 John 3:17 and James 1:27.

Wesley: 'thou hast no pity for thy friend — a plain evidence thou wantest the fear of God'; Clarke prefers the Vulgate and notes the variant 'to him that despiseth his friend' (with Mr. Good), aimed at Eliphaz.

Ellicott finds the dependent clauses hard: rather 'even to one that forsaketh the fear of the Almighty,' or 'lest he should forsake' it — unpitied misery may tempt the sufferer himself to cast off religion.

debates.question: Who forsakes the fear of the Almighty?

sides.position: the friend who withholds pity has abandoned the fear of God
the afflicted man, who unpitied may be driven to forsake it (or pity owed even to such)

themes: the crux of the second clause

schools.summary: Gill: the brethren are kin by shared religion among idolaters — which aggravates their treachery; a brook fed by rains and melting snow, swelling then failing.
Henry: the deceit is the frustrating of just expectations — they came by appointment to mourn, yet poured vinegar into his wounds; wisdom to cease from man and trust the rock of ages.

Clarke describes the land torrents that promise a lasting stream and fail in the sand — physicians of no value; Wesley notes all three friends are 'brethren' who added to the afflictions they came to remove.

Ellicott calls it one of the book's most celebrated similes, recalling the Guadalquivir at Cordova shrunk in August; Keil and Delitzsch render 'as the stream of brooks they pass away' and note the disputed 'paths'/'caravans' word.

Gill: streams frozen over look blackish (a black frost) — either Job's household in black circumstances, or (rather) the friends, foul waters iced over, their true colour and blackness of heart hidden.

Clarke: waters suddenly frozen, foam like snow, speedily melted and lost to evaporation and thirsty sand; Wesley: full in winter when the traveller needs it least, filled by accidental falls, not a constant spring.
Henry keeps the flood-picture: the brooks make a great show swollen with melted ice and snow, blackish and muddy — the show matching the friends' large promise.

themes: blackish by reason of the ice
a promise the summer will break

schools.summary: Gill: the ice and snow melt and vanish with the warmth; so the friends ceased to be friends when the sun of affliction looked on Job.
Wesley marks the two stages — 'wax warm' as the weather softens, then the hot season when water is most needed and they are consumed out of their place.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'it becometh hot, they are extinguished from their place' — the stream snuffed out where it lay.
Henry: when the high are sunk and need comfort, those who once gathered about them stand aloof and run them down.

themes: what time they wax warm they vanish
dry when the need is real

schools.summary: Gill reads it of the waters — melted, they run off in windings till wholly lost, as every trace of the friends' friendship is gone.
Clarke: torrents forsake their channels (as the Ganges), divide, dwindle, and perish in the sands; Wesley: gone out of their channel, flowing hither and thither till consumed.
Keil and Delitzsch point the word as 'caravans' that turn aside and perish in the waste; Ellicott lays both possibilities side by side and, from the next verse, favours the caravans.

debates.question: Is it the streams that are lost or the caravans that perish?

sides.position: the streams wander off and vanish in the sand
the caravans turn aside from their course and perish

themes: friends both torrent and cause of straying

schools.summary: Gill: Tema, a city of Arabia named from Ishmael's son, whose caravans looked to the winter waters to supply their summer thirst.

Clarke: the caravans arrive full of expectation to slake thirst and fill their water-skins, and find the waters lost; Wesley: Tema and Sheba lie in hot dry Arabia, travellers moving in companies for safety.

Ellicott cites Fürst on Tema (a tract on the desert's northern edge, cf. Isa. 21:14; Jer. 25:23) and Sheba (a trafficking, plundering district, cf. Job 1:15); Keil and Delitzsch render 'the travelling bands of Tema looked, the caravans of Saba hoped.'
Henry catches the travellers' murmured hope — 'a little further, there was water enough' — the confident expectation Job means.

themes: the troops of Tema and Sheba
the surer the hope, the crueller the loss

schools.summary: Gill: coming and finding no water, the travellers are confounded and ashamed of a hope built on a groundless surmise.
Wesley: they had comforted themselves with expectation and are ashamed as men who deceived themselves and others — we prepare confusion by vain hopes, and the reeds break because we lean on them.
Ellicott compares Jeremiah's famine (Jer. 14:3), the vessels returned empty; Keil and Delitzsch: 'disappointed on account of their trust, they came thus far and were red with shame.'
Henry: the greater the confidence in the creature, the greater the confusion when it fails; wiser to make God our confidence.
Gill notes the two readings — 'ye are nothing' or (marginal, with Jarchi) 'ye are like it,' the brook — and Broughton's union of both, 'ye are become like that, even nothing.'

Keil and Delitzsch judge the Keri to yield no sense and the written word, a noun of negation, to give the point — 'ye are become nothing' (Targum: 'as though ye had never been'); Ellicott records both readings without forcing a choice.

Clarke: the friends are to Job what the torrents were to the caravans — nothing; they see his casting down and start back terrified; Wesley probes the fear — shy of him lest a further plague involve them or he prove a burden.
Henry: once they were something to Job, now nothing but God.

debates.question: Is the reading 'ye are nothing' or 'ye are like it [the brook]'?

sides.position: 'ye are become nothing' (the written text, a negation)
'ye are like it' — the failed brook (the marginal reading)

themes: ye see my casting down and are afraid

schools.summary: Gill: did Job ever invite them to bring presents to support him? He asked no such thing.
Henry: though needy Job was not craving nor burdensome — he sought no collection though ruined and once charitable; a good man fears to be troublesome, as Paul worked not to burden any.
Clarke: why stand aloof — has he demanded presents or supply from their stores? Wesley: he asked nothing for his support, they might at least have given comfortable words.
Ellicott: Job never laid himself under obligation nor asked their help before, so cannot be convicted of abusing their kindness; Keil and Delitzsch open the run of things Job never sought.

themes: did I say, Bring unto me

schools.summary: Gill: 'the enemy' may be rendered 'the hand of straitness,' the tribulation pressing him on every side, from which he never summoned them to rescue him.

Wesley distinguishes 'deliver' (rescue by arms, as Abraham delivered Lot) from 'redeem' (ransom by price); Clarke: did he send for them to avenge him of the Sabeans and Chaldeans or recover his substance?
Henry: Job did not urge them to raise the country or make reprisals — 'I will rather sit content under my affliction than sponge upon my friends.'
Keil and Delitzsch let the couplet stand as the second and third demands Job never made — deliverance from the foe and redemption from the tyrant.

themes: rescue by arms or by ransom

schools.summary: Gill: the mark of a humble, teachable mind — Job will hear in silence, weigh, and if convinced hold his peace, willing to learn even from unkind friends.
Clarke: show me where I am mistaken by proper arguments, and I shall gladly abandon my errors; Wesley: convince me by solid arguments and I will patiently hear and gladly receive counsel.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'Teach me, and I will be silent, and cause me to understand wherein I have failed' — silence bound to the condition of real instruction.
Henry: Job is not obstinate but ready to strike sail to truth, if they give plain instruction instead of invidious reflection.

themes: teach me and I will hold my tongue

schools.summary: Gill: 'right words' are strong, 'bony' arguments according to right reason, above all the Scriptures of truth, which carry conviction and bear men down.

Keil and Delitzsch weigh the variant sense 'how sweet' (cf. Ps. 119:103, with Hirzel, Ewald, Schlottmann) but find it unsuited to the book's usage, and set aside Hupfeld's and Hahn's construals; Ellicott renders 'words of uprightness' and hears the proverb that open rebuke is better than secret love.

Clarke: a well-built argument on truth is irresistible, but 'what reproof is in a reproof from you?' — no fault proved, no vice reproved; notes the variant 'how savoury'; Wesley: no truth in their assertions nor weight in their arguments.
Henry: fair reasoning has commanding power, railing is impotent; the friends' hypothesis is false, their surmises groundless, their application peevish.

sides.position: 'how forcible are right words' (the received text)
'how sweet/savoury' (variant nimletsu)
holders: Hirzel and Ewald (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

themes: open rebuke better than secret love

schools.summary: Gill: do they run him down with bare words, or catch at expressions uttered in distress to make him an offender for a phrase, having no fact of his life to charge?

Clarke: they catch at some expression let fall under unprecedented affliction, finding no flaw in his conduct; Wesley: no allowance for infirmity or misery — the words of a hopeless man, 'as wind' that passes and is forgotten.
Ellicott: it cannot be their intent to reprove mere words, confessedly rash (v.3), hardly worth the trouble; Keil and Delitzsch: 'the words of one in despair belong to the wind.'
Henry: they contrive to reprove passionate expressions as marks of atheism, where candour would excuse them; shall a man's spiritual state be judged by words extorted by trouble?

themes: the speeches of one desperate are as wind
convicting the grief, not the life

schools.summary: Gill takes the fatherless to be Job himself, stripped and given to Satan, the verb 'ye cause to fall upon the fatherless' — wrath, a weight, or (Broughton) a net to entrap him in talk.

Clarke: as destitute as an orphan — would they overwhelm such a one? — and 'dig a pit' is to lay wait and entangle him; Wesley: 'overwhelm' is to load with censures, 'the fatherless' the desolate man they cast down.

Ellicott prefers, for the parallelism, 'Ye would cast lots upon the fatherless, and make merchandise of your friend'; Keil and Delitzsch render likewise, 'cast lots for the orphan, and traffic about your friend.'
Henry: 'overwhelm the fatherless' is proverbial for the most barbarous conduct; and 'dig a pit for your friend' is to ensnare under colour of friendship, making his free speech the trap.

debates.question: Is the rendering 'overwhelm the fatherless / dig a pit' or 'cast lots upon the fatherless / make merchandise of your friend'?

sides.position: 'ye overwhelm the fatherless, and dig a pit for your friend' (received)
'ye cast lots upon the fatherless, and make merchandise of your friend' (parallelism)

themes: dig a pit for your friend
the lowest point of the reproach

schools.summary: Gill catches the courtesy: 'be content' is 'may it please you' — a respectful entreaty for a favourable look and a fresh hearing, sure he would be acquitted.
Clarke: view me, consider my circumstances, compare my words, and be convinced I speak truth; Wesley: look on my cause more carefully, that you may give a more righteous verdict.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'be pleased to observe me keenly; I will not deceive you to your face,' the word meaning to scrutinize; Ellicott: 'for surely I shall not lie to your face.'
Henry: what do you see that bespeaks me a madman or wicked? Look in my face for a submissive spirit, or on my ulcers, and it is evident I do not lie — do not complain without cause.

themes: I will not lie to your face

schools.summary: Gill: a plea to return from their ill opinion to juster sentiments, or literally to return to their seats and hear the cause out.
Henry reads a call to a rehearing without prejudice — a just cause desires nothing more than a just hearing, and Job keeps his integrity though not his temper.
Clarke: reconsider the whole subject, be not offended — 'my righteousness is in it,' my argumentation itself proving my innocence; Wesley: turn from your former judgment, the right is on Job's side.

Keil and Delitzsch: the imperative is 'begin afresh,' not 'retrace your steps' — let there be no injustice, Job's righteousness still stands; Ellicott: try once more before deciding there is unrighteousness in Job, or in his tongue.

themes: a plea for justice, not mercy

schools.summary: Gill: 'iniquity in my tongue' of his words, though he owns the tongue is a world of iniquity and the best of men offend in word.

Clarke: am I not honest? would not conscience discern a falsehood, and would such a man defend a known wrong? — the whole chapter an inimitable apology that might have ended the controversy had the friends not prejudged him; Wesley: 'taste' is the judgment, trying words as the palate tries meats.

Ellicott turns the question on the friends' condescension — Job knows what is right as well as they, with no more vicious reasoning, probably less — and owns how hard it is to trace the thread of Job's argument from chapter to chapter.

themes: is there iniquity in my tongue
the case left open by prejudice
